profilePeriod: Political record centred on the 1979–1990 premiership; dated 1969 and 1978 statements provide earlier context. The 2002 book is a reading recommendation, not a substitute for the governing record.
scopeNote: Question answers are source-constrained simulations, not claims that Thatcher took this quiz. Contemporary hypotheticals require explicit inference from her principles and policies.

sources.title: UK government biography
sources.evidence: Premiership, privatisation, deregulation, union reform and the Falklands War.

sources.title: Conservative election manifesto 1979
sources.evidence: Parliamentary rule of law, monetary discipline, lower taxes, property ownership, union ballots, stronger policing, immigration controls and retained NHS funding.

sources.title: Conservative election manifesto 1983
sources.evidence: Privatisation of named firms, competition with consumer safeguards, retained public health services, council rate limits and abolition of metropolitan councils; NATO, nuclear deterrence and negotiated arms control.

sources.title: Granada World in Action interview
sources.evidence: Restrictive immigration and cultural assimilation; distinguish criticism of migration levels from equal treatment of lawful residents.

sources.title: BBC Nationwide interview
sources.evidence: Personally supports capital punishment as deterrence; does not claim executions were restored under her government.

sources.title: Conservative Party conference speech
sources.evidence: Traditional sexual morality, national curriculum, parental school choice and state-funded independent schools; police and security forces framed as safeguarding liberty.

sources.title: Sermon on the Mound
sources.evidence: Publicly links Christianity to personal responsibility, human rights and democracy; distinguishes legislative rule of law from the church’s spiritual teaching.

sources.title: Bruges speech
sources.evidence: Opposes a European superstate while supporting cooperation, the single market and reduced world trade barriers.

sources.title: Royal Society speech
sources.evidence: Supports scientific progress and basic research while recognising environmental limits and greenhouse warming.

sources.title: UN General Assembly environmental speech
sources.evidence: International climate cooperation, scientific assessment and sustainable development; does not advocate rejecting industrial civilisation.

sources.title: Foundation biography: later writings
sources.evidence: Statecraft was first published in 2002 and discusses international politics.

sources.title: Brazilian library catalogue: Statecraft translation
sources.evidence: Brazilian title: A arte de governar: estratégias para um mundo em mudança; this edition date does not replace the original publication year.

sources.title: Wikimedia Commons portrait and permissions
sources.evidence: Commons records permission from the Thatcher Estate for unrestricted reuse; photograph is a stock portrait, photographer unidentified.

sources.title: Finchley Inter-church luncheon speech, reported in Finchley Press
sources.evidence: Supports compulsory religious education but acknowledges abortion reform reduced dangerous illegal procedures; private immorality does not automatically justify unenforceable criminal prohibitions.

sources.title: Speech to Conservative Central Council
sources.evidence: Supports nuclear deterrence and reciprocal negotiation, explicitly hoping the younger generation will not be called up to fight. The professional-force interpretation is an inference from her governing record, not a quotation from this speech.

sources.title: Lawson minute proposing Bank of England independence
sources.evidence: A proposal for central-bank independence, not a policy already implemented by Thatcher.

sources.title: House of Lords: Bank of England role
sources.evidence: Government remains ultimately responsible for monetary policy while the Bank advises and implements it.

sources.title: House of Commons: Abortion (Amendment) Bill
sources.evidence: Debate records the Prime Minister favouring a 24-week limit, distinguishing this from Alton’s 18-week proposal.

sources.title: Bernard Ingham press digest for the Prime Minister, page 5
sources.evidence: Contemporaneous digest records opposition to the 18-week proposal and preference for 24 weeks.

estrutura.interpretation: Unitary UK parliamentary authority, national standards and council spending restraints; borough-level service transfers and school autonomy qualify centralisation. Opposition to EU centralisation is not support for a federal UK.

representacao.interpretation: Representative parliamentary democracy and individual rights; strong executive leadership within elections, not dictatorship or direct democracy.

poder.interpretation: Firm law and order, punitive deterrence and anti-terrorism, qualified by rule of law and civil rights.

imigracao.interpretation: Controlled migration and cultural assimilation with equal legal treatment, not racial supremacy.

diplomacia.interpretation: Strong defence, NATO and nuclear deterrence, balanced by negotiated arms control rather than unlimited war.

intervencao.interpretation: Assertive defence of British sovereignty and overseas interests, including the Falklands; international alliances rather than isolation.

economia.interpretation: Private enterprise and privatisation with continuing public health provision and a welfare safety net; not abolition of all public services.

controle.interpretation: Competition, monetary restraint and opposition to price controls, while retaining consumer protection and some public spending; not laissez-faire anarchism. During her premiership monetary responsibility remained with government; deregulation does not imply an operationally independent or abolished central bank.

comercio.interpretation: Free trade and the European single market despite opposition to supranational political government; sovereignty is not blanket protectionism.

religiao.interpretation: Christian moral grounding in public politics, with religious tolerance and separate roles for Parliament and churches; not clerical government.

moral.interpretation: Traditional family and sexual values with individual responsibility; a female prime minister is not automatically a progressive social platform. Her 1969 acknowledgement of safer legal abortion qualifies any inference of blanket prohibition.

tecnologia.interpretation: Science, industry and technological development with environmental safeguards; no basis for equating modernisation with unlimited transhumanism.

nearestProfileDistinctions: Reagan governed a federal presidential system; Thatcher governed a unitary parliamentary UK.
Friedman was an economic thinker; Thatcher exercised executive authority with policing, defence and public-service responsibilities.
Blair shared some market reforms but differed in social values and territorial devolution.
